{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "plan@1",
  "goal": "Implement the Prism evaluation and quality gating platform and Lumen session intelligence engine across 6 modular Rust workspace crates.",
  "architecture": "Implements a layered safe Rust monorepo starting from Layer 1 permissive primitives (lumen-model) through zero-copy streaming ingestion (lumen-session), 22 single-pass accumulators and petgraph Trajectory DAG analysis (lumen-analysis, lumen-pattern), and decoupled 4-engine evaluation suites with VCR replay (prism-core, prism-grader), exposed via standalone pre-compiled CLI binaries.",
  "tech_stack": [
    "Rust 1.80+",
    "simd-json",
    "rayon",
    "memmap2",
    "petgraph",
    "compact_str",
    "smallvec",
    "clap",
    "miette",
    "reqwest",
    "tokio",
    "tempfile",
    "serde_json",
    "jsonschema"
  ],
  "batches": [
    {
      "batch_id": "BATCH-01",
      "title": "Layer 1: Canonical Domain Primitives & Pricing",
      "target_crate": "lumen-model",
      "task_ids": ["TASK-001", "TASK-002"]
    },
    {
      "batch_id": "BATCH-02",
      "title": "Layer 1.5: Multi-Orchestrator Ingestion & SIMD Parser",
      "target_crate": "lumen-session",
      "task_ids": ["TASK-003", "TASK-004"]
    },
    {
      "batch_id": "BATCH-03",
      "title": "Layer 2: 22 Accumulators & Trajectory DAG Graph Engine",
      "target_crate": "lumen-analysis",
      "task_ids": ["TASK-005", "TASK-006", "TASK-007"]
    },
    {
      "batch_id": "BATCH-04",
      "title": "Layer 3: Evaluation Core, VCR Cassettes & The 4 Graders",
      "target_crate": "prism-grader",
      "task_ids": ["TASK-008", "TASK-009", "TASK-010"]
    },
    {
      "batch_id": "BATCH-05",
      "title": "Layer 4: Standalone CLIs, Config & GitHub Actions CI",
      "target_crate": "prism-cli",
      "task_ids": ["TASK-011", "TASK-012"]
    }
  ],
  "tasks": [
    {
      "id": "TASK-001",
      "title": "Implement Canonical IR, Turn, ToolIntent, and Timing Models",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-model/Cargo.toml",
          "crates/lumen-model/src/lib.rs",
          "crates/lumen-model/src/transcript.rs",
          "crates/lumen-model/src/turn.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["Cargo.toml"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-model/tests/test_transcript.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [
        "1. Define Root workspace Cargo.toml with resolver = '2' and workspace members.",
        "2. Implement CanonicalTranscript, CanonicalTurn, ToolIntent, and TurnRole with compact_str and smallvec in crates/lumen-model/src/transcript.rs.",
        "3. Write unit tests in crates/lumen-model/tests/test_transcript.rs verifying serialization roundtrips.",
        "4. Run `cargo test -p lumen-model` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-model): define canonical transcript, turn, and tool intent primitives",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-001"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-002",
      "title": "Implement Exact Mathematical Token Economics and Model Pricing Matrix",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-model/src/pricing.rs",
          "crates/lumen-model/src/economics.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["crates/lumen-model/src/lib.rs"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-model/tests/test_pricing.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [
        "1. Implement ModelPricing struct with 4-tier rates (input_base, cache_write 1.25x, cache_read 0.10x, output) for Sonnet, Haiku, Opus, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek.",
        "2. Implement TokenEconomics calculation for cache_hit_ratio, baseline_cost_no_cache_usd, and financial efficiency_multiplier.",
        "3. Write tests in crates/lumen-model/tests/test_pricing.rs verifying billing math against official Anthropic rates.",
        "4. Run `cargo test -p lumen-model` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-model): implement prompt cache pricing matrix and economics calculations",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-002", "CRIT-PRISM-003"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-003",
      "title": "Implement SessionAdapter Trait and Auto-Fingerprint Ingestion Engine",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-session/Cargo.toml",

          "crates/lumen-session/src/fingerprint.rs"

        "modify": ["Cargo.toml"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-session/tests/test_fingerprint.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [

        "2. Implement fast sub-millisecond fingerprint detector inspecting first 2KB of log bytes.",
        "3. Write unit tests in crates/lumen-session/tests/test_fingerprint.rs verifying detection of Claude Code, AGY, and Codex logs.",
        "4. Run `cargo test -p lumen-session` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-session): implement SessionAdapter trait and orchestrator fingerprinting",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-001", "CRIT-PRISM-022"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-004",
      "title": "Implement SIMD-Accelerated ClaudeCodeAdapter and PreCompact Snapshot Merging",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-session/src/adapters/claude.rs",
          "crates/lumen-session/src/snapshot.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["crates/lumen-session/src/lib.rs"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-session/tests/test_claude_adapter.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [
        "1. Implement ClaudeCodeAdapter using simd-json and memory-mapped reader.",
        "2. Implement PreCompact snapshot merge taking max() over cumulative tokens.",
        "3. Write test verifying handling of corrupt lines and non-destructive snapshot merging.",
        "4. Run `cargo test -p lumen-session` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-session): implement simd-json Claude adapter and pre-compact snapshot merge",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-001", "CRIT-PRISM-005", "CRIT-PRISM-022"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-005",
      "title": "Implement the 22 Single-Pass Streaming Accumulators",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-analysis/Cargo.toml",
          "crates/lumen-analysis/src/lib.rs",
          "crates/lumen-analysis/src/accumulators.rs",
          "crates/lumen-analysis/src/token_usage.rs",
          "crates/lumen-analysis/src/circuit_breaker.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["Cargo.toml"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-analysis/tests/test_accumulators.rs"]

        "3. Write tests verifying single-pass O(N) extraction with 0 heap allocations in inner loop.",
        "4. Run `cargo test -p lumen-analysis` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-analysis): implement 22 single-pass streaming accumulators",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-001", "CRIT-PRISM-008", "CRIT-PRISM-009"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-006",
      "title": "Implement TrajectoryGraph and Tarjan SCC Cycle Detection Engine",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-pattern/Cargo.toml",
          "crates/lumen-pattern/src/lib.rs",
          "crates/lumen-pattern/src/graph.rs",
          "crates/lumen-pattern/src/scc.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["Cargo.toml"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-pattern/tests/test_trajectory_loops.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [
        "1. Implement TrajectoryGraph using petgraph::graph::DiGraph with ToolNode elements.",
        "2. Implement Tarjan SCC cycle detector identifying exploration loops of depth >= 3 without state mutations.",
        "3. Implement Trajectory Efficiency Index calculation E = (Mutations + Targeted Reads) / Invocations.",
        "4. Write tests verifying circular loop detection on real agent search traces.",
        "5. Run `cargo test -p lumen-pattern` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-pattern): implement petgraph Trajectory DAG and Tarjan SCC cycle detector",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-006", "CRIT-PRISM-007", "CRIT-PRISM-025"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-007",
      "title": "Implement Multi-Session Parallel Directory Scanner using Rayon and Memmap2",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/lumen-analysis/src/scanner.rs",
          "crates/lumen-analysis/src/summary.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["crates/lumen-analysis/src/lib.rs"],
        "test": ["crates/lumen-analysis/tests/test_parallel_scan.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [
        "1. Implement parallel_scan_sessions using rayon par_iter and memmap2.",
        "2. Parse multi-session directory trees into aggregated summaries in parallel.",
        "3. Write integration test scanning 50 mock session logs in under 100ms.",
        "4. Run `cargo test -p lumen-analysis` and confirm GREEN."
      ],
      "commit_message": "feat(lumen-analysis): implement rayon parallel multi-session scanner",
      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-019"]
    },
    {
      "id": "TASK-008",
      "title": "Implement TaskSpec, Scorecard, VCR Cassettes, and Hermetic Sandbox",
      "files": {
        "create": [
          "crates/prism-core/Cargo.toml",
          "crates/prism-core/src/lib.rs",
          "crates/prism-core/src/task.rs",
          "crates/prism-core/src/vcr.rs",
          "crates/prism-core/src/sandbox.rs"
        ],
        "modify": ["Cargo.toml"],
        "test": ["crates/prism-core/tests/test_sandbox_vcr.rs"]
      },
      "steps": [

      "covers_criteria": ["CRIT-PRISM-014", "CRIT-PRISM-015", "CRIT-PRISM-018", "CRIT-PRISM-024"]

This is a much bigger job than it first looked — two of the three crates are substantially unfinished relative to their specs, and several pieces require real design decisions before I write code. Quick picture of what I found:

**prism-core**: drivers (Claude/AGY/OpenAI-compatible/OpenCode/VCR) are solidly implemented. `WorkspaceSandbox` is a stub — just `cp -r` + `git init`, missing the spec'd Reflink/APFS CoW cloning, POSIX process-group reaping/timeout, and `git_checkout`/`apply_patch`/`run_test_suite` methods entirely. Also found a real bug: `OpenCodeDriver` parses OpenCode's output with `ClaudeCodeAdapter` instead of the `OpenCodeAdapter` that now exists in lumen-session.

**prism-grader**: 3 of 4 graders exist (RedGreen, Trajectory, CircuitBreaker) but `RedGreenGrader` doesn't actually implement the `Grader` trait the spec defines. `CalibratedJudge` (the Opus rubric grader) doesn't exist at all — zero code.

**prism-cli**: this is the roughest part. `prism test` builds a fake in-memory transcript with empty turns and never invokes any real driver or sandbox. `prism bench` prints **hardcoded literal numbers** ("62.5%", "$0.42") — not computed from anything. `prism rebuild` and `prism record` are pure `println!` stubs. `prism matrix` — the subcommand the spec requires — doesn't exist in the CLI at all, even though `MatrixResultDatum`/`MetricDifferential` are already built in prism-grader. No TOML config loading, no suite-file format/loader, no OTel/Parquet/GitHub-summary exporters exist (`toml` is a declared dependency but unused; there's no `opentelemetry` or `parquet` dependency at all). And `rebuild` as a command has zero corresponding acceptance criteria anywhere in the specs — it's pure invention sitting in the code.

Given the size and the number of real design decisions in here (how `CalibratedJudge` actually calls out to Claude, what the matrix/suite TOML schemas look like, whether to build OTel/Parquet now or stub them, what to do with the unspec'd `rebuild` command), I want to lay out a sequenced plan before writing code rather than starting to type.

# Prism Architecture: Core Evaluation Models, VCR Cassettes & Sandboxing (`01-core-evaluation-and-vcr-cassettes.md`)

This document defines the core evaluation data models, VCR cassette record/replay engine, and workspace sandboxing in `crates/prism-core`.

## 1. Domain Models

pub struct TaskSpec {
    pub id: CompactString,
    pub skill: CompactString,
    pub input_prompt: String,
    pub fixture_repo: Option<PathBuf>,
    pub expected_assertions: Vec<CompactString>,
    pub max_turns: usize,

}

pub struct VcrCassette {
    pub task_id: CompactString,
    pub prompt_hash: CompactString,
    pub transcript: CanonicalTranscript,
}
```

---

## 2. Execution Drivers

1. **`ClaudeCliDriver` / `AgyCliDriver`**: Spawns local CLI in non-interactive mode. Zero API keys needed; uses developer's active login session.
2. **`AnthropicApiDriver`**: Direct HTTPS Messages API with `anthropic-beta: prompt-caching-2024-07-31` headers.
3. **`VcrReplayDriver`**: Replays frozen cassettes in $<5\text{ms}$ with $\$0.00$ API spend.

---

## 3. Hermetic Sandboxing (`WorkspaceSandbox`)

- Clones fixture repository into isolated `/tmp/prism_sandbox_*/` directory.
- Initializes clean ephemeral Git repository.
- Evaluates test state transitions without polluting host workspace.
- Cleans up automatically on drop.

# Prism Architecture: The 4 Decoupled Evaluation Grader Engines (`02-the-four-grader-engines.md`)

This document defines the 4 evaluation grading engines in `crates/prism-grader`.

---

## 1. Grader Engine Architecture

```rust
pub trait Grader: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn evaluate(
        &self,
        spec: &TaskSpec,
        transcript: &CanonicalTranscript,
    ) -> Result<AssertionResult, EvaluationError>;
}
```

---

## 2. The 4 Graders

1. **`RedGreenGrader`**: SWE-bench style state transition verification. Asserts test suite FAILS before patch (Red Pass) and PASSES with zero regressions after patch (Green Pass).
2. **`TrajectoryGrader`**: Asserts prompt cache hit ratio $\ge 90.0\%$ and zero circular Tarjan SCC exploration loops.
3. **`CircuitBreakerGrader`**: Asserts multi-agent review iterations (Drafter ↔ Auditor) reach consensus in $\le 2$ rounds.
4. **`CalibratedJudge`**: Evaluates formative G-Eval rubrics with Opus using contrastive pass/fail few-shot anchors.

---

## 3. Output Schema

All grading engines assemble their findings into [`shared/schemas/eval-report@1.json`](file:///Users/gabe/Projects/agent-plugins/shared/schemas/eval-report@1.json).

This document defines the CLI commands, TOML configuration schema, and CI/CD pipelines in `crates/prism-cli`.

---

## 1. CLI Commands

- `prism test [suite]`: Runs ultra-fast offline CI regression suite using local VCR cassettes.
- `prism bench --skill=<SKILL>`: Runs Tessl-style "Skill Lift" A/B benchmarks against baseline models.
- `prism rebuild --fixture=<DIR>`: Runs the Rebuild Test (reconstructing repository from `spec@1` alone).
- `prism record --task=<TASK>`: Records golden VCR cassettes from live completions.
- `prism validate [DIR]`: Validates plugin manifests and Draft-07 schemas.

---

## 2. Configuration (`prism.toml`)

```toml
[eval]
default_suite = "all"
default_driver = "auto"
cassettes_dir = "tests/cassettes"
fixtures_dir = "tests/fixtures"

[invariants]
min_cache_hit_ratio = 0.90
max_circuit_rounds = 2
min_trajectory_efficiency = 0.85
fail_on_circular_loops = true
```

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflows

- `.github/workflows/eval-pr.yml`: Executes `prism test --offline --github-summary` on every PR (<10s runtime, $0.00 API spend).
- `.github/workflows/eval-nightly.yml`: Runs live frontier Skill Lift matrix benchmarks on schedule.
- `.github/workflows/update-cassettes.yml`: Automatically re-records golden cassettes when PR is labeled `update-cassettes`.

1	# Multi-Dimensional Matrix Evaluation & Empirical Differentials (`docs/04`)
2	
3	This document defines the 8 empirical evaluation dimensions, Cartesian matrix execution engine, and statistical percentage differential ($\Delta$) formulas of Prism.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. The 8 Evaluated Dimensions
8	
9	Prism evaluates every trial across 8 empirical dimensions:
10	
11	| Dimension | Metric Unit | Calculation Formula | Purpose |
12	| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
13	| **1. Pass Rate** | `%` | `(passed_assertions / total_assertions) * 100.0` | Functional correctness & zero regressions. |
14	| **2. Cache Hit Ratio** | `%` | $H = \frac{I_{\text{read}}}{I_{\text{uncached}} + I_{\text{write}} + I_{\text{read}}} \times 100.0$ | Prompt cache health & prefix stability. |
15	| **3. Financial Cost** | `USD $` | Exact 4-tier spend ($P_{\text{in}}, P_{\text{write}}, P_{\text{read}}, P_{\text{out}}$) | Monetary cost per task trial. |
16	| **4. Turns** | `Count` | Total user, assistant, and tool turns | Directness of resolution vs wandering. |
17	| **5. Turn Latency** | `ms` | p50 & p95 percentiles of turn completions | API responsiveness and tool overhead. |
18	| **6. Total Wall Time** | `ms` / `s` | $\sum_{t=1}^N \text{latency}(t)$ | Total developer wait time. |
19	| **7. Token Volumes** | `Tokens` | Total prompt input + completion output | Context inflation & prompt verbosity. |
20	| **8. Quality Score** | `[0.0 - 1.0]` | Grounding ($\mathcal{G}$) + Monotonicity ($M$) + Rubric | Solution elegance & zero cyclic loops. |
21	
22	---
23	
24	## 2. Same-vs-Same Empirical Differentials
25	
26	To eliminate anecdotal guessing, Prism calculates exact percentage deltas ($\Delta$) against baseline controls:
27	
28	```rust
29	// crates/prism-grader/src/matrix.rs
30	pub struct MetricDifferential {
31	    pub delta_pass_rate_pct: f32,    // e.g. +36.0%
32	    pub delta_cost_pct: f32,         // e.g. -66.7% (Savings)
33	    pub delta_turns_pct: f32,        // e.g. -63.4% (Fewer turns)
34	    pub delta_cache_hit_pct: f32,    // e.g. +49.3% (Higher cache hit)
35	    pub delta_latency_p95_pct: f32,  // e.g. -42.1% (Faster turns)
36	    pub delta_wall_time_pct: f32,    // e.g. -55.0% (Faster completion)
37	    pub delta_quality_score_pct: f32,// e.g. +22.5% (Higher quality)
38	}
39	```
40	
41	---
42	
43	## 3. Commercial API vs. Self-Hosted Zero-Token Costing
44	
45	* **Commercial APIs**: Exact 4-tier billing per million tokens ($P_{\text{in}}, P_{\text{write}}, P_{\text{read}}, P_{\text{out}}$).
46	* **Local & On-Prem Models (Qwen, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM)**: Reported as **`$0.00 (API Token Fees) / Self-Hosted`**, while tracking real physical compute metrics (Wall Time, Latency p95, Token Volumes, and Turns).
47

# Multi-Dimensional Matrix Evaluation & Empirical Differentials (`docs/04`)

This document defines the 8 empirical evaluation dimensions, Cartesian matrix execution engine, and statistical percentage differential ($\Delta$) formulas of Prism.

---

## 1. The 8 Evaluated Dimensions

Prism evaluates every trial across 8 empirical dimensions:

| Dimension | Metric Unit | Calculation Formula | Purpose |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Pass Rate** | `%` | `(passed_assertions / total_assertions) * 100.0` | Functional correctness & zero regressions. |
| **2. Cache Hit Ratio** | `%` | $H = \frac{I_{\text{read}}}{I_{\text{uncached}} + I_{\text{write}} + I_{\text{read}}} \times 100.0$ | Prompt cache health & prefix stability. |
| **3. Financial Cost** | `USD $` | Exact 4-tier spend ($P_{\text{in}}, P_{\text{write}}, P_{\text{read}}, P_{\text{out}}$) | Monetary cost per task trial. |
| **4. Turns** | `Count` | Total user, assistant, and tool turns | Directness of resolution vs wandering. |
| **5. Turn Latency** | `ms` | p50 & p95 percentiles of turn completions | API responsiveness and tool overhead. |
| **6. Total Wall Time** | `ms` / `s` | $\sum_{t=1}^N \text{latency}(t)$ | Total developer wait time. |
| **7. Token Volumes** | `Tokens` | Total prompt input + completion output | Context inflation & prompt verbosity. |
| **8. Quality Score** | `[0.0 - 1.0]` | Grounding ($\mathcal{G}$) + Monotonicity ($M$) + Rubric | Solution elegance & zero cyclic loops. |

---

## 2. Same-vs-Same Empirical Differentials

To eliminate anecdotal guessing, Prism calculates exact percentage deltas ($\Delta$) against baseline controls:

```rust
// crates/prism-grader/src/matrix.rs
pub struct MetricDifferential {
    pub delta_pass_rate_pct: f32,    // e.g. +36.0%
    pub delta_cost_pct: f32,         // e.g. -66.7% (Savings)
    pub delta_turns_pct: f32,        // e.g. -63.4% (Fewer turns)
    pub delta_cache_hit_pct: f32,    // e.g. +49.3% (Higher cache hit)
    pub delta_latency_p95_pct: f32,  // e.g. -42.1% (Faster turns)
    pub delta_wall_time_pct: f32,    // e.g. -55.0% (Faster completion)
    pub delta_quality_score_pct: f32,// e.g. +22.5% (Higher quality)
}
```

---

## 3. Commercial API vs. Self-Hosted Zero-Token Costing

* **Commercial APIs**: Exact 4-tier billing per million tokens ($P_{\text{in}}, P_{\text{write}}, P_{\text{read}}, P_{\text{out}}$).
* **Local & On-Prem Models (Qwen, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM)**: Reported as **`$0.00 (API Token Fees) / Self-Hosted`**, while tracking real physical compute metrics (Wall Time, Latency p95, Token Volumes, and Turns).

I've now confirmed a pattern that mirrors what we found in Lumen: several pieces of Prism's spec **scope line** name a capability, but zero acceptance criteria back it up anywhere — meaning nothing testable was ever defined for them, and in one case the referenced schema file doesn't even exist:

- **`CalibratedJudge`** (the 4th grader, Opus-based rubric grading) — named in the README/docs, but has **no `api_surface` entry and no acceptance criteria** in `SPEC-PRISM-002-GRADER.json` at all. It would need a real design: how it calls out to Claude, rubric format, contrastive anchors — none of that is specified anywhere.
- **OTel OTLP exporter + Apache Parquet sink** — named in `SPEC-PRISM-003-CLI.json`'s scope line, but again **zero acceptance criteria**, and no `opentelemetry`/`parquet` crate is even in `Cargo.toml`.
- **`eval-report@1.json`** — `docs/02` says all graders conform to this schema at a path in the sibling `agent-plugins` repo. I checked: **that file doesn't exist anywhere.** `build_eval_report` currently just emits an ad hoc JSON blob with nothing to validate against, so `CRIT-PRISM-127` ("100% validates against eval-report@1") is currently unsatisfiable.
- **`prism rebuild`** and **`prism validate`** — both appear in `docs/03` and (rebuild) in the actual CLI code, but neither has a single acceptance criterion in `SPEC-PRISM-003-CLI.json`'s scope line or criteria. `rebuild`'s description ("reconstruct a repository from spec@1 alone") is really a full autonomous-coding-agent loop, not a mechanical CLI feature — and today it's a `println!` stub that claims fake success.

I want your call on these before I lock in the plan, since each has real cost/design implications.

# Lumen: Comprehensive Spec/Doc Gap-Filling

## Context

An earlier 4-way audit (core code vs. docs, infra/CLI vs. docs, adversarial spec quality, strategy-doc scrutiny) found that Lumen's specs and docs systematically overclaim relative to what's built and, in several places, are internally inconsistent or untestable as written:

- **SPEC-005-ANALYSIS**: only 8 of the "22 accumulators" have acceptance criteria at all (some implemented accumulators like `artifacts`/`autonomy`/`context_growth`/`stats`/`tool_inventory` aren't even covered; 9 more — `flow`, `hook_activity`, `pr_link`, `fuzzy_tools`, `attribution`, `timeline`, `otel_correlation`, `span_mapping`, `trajectory_dag` — don't exist as code or criteria). PLAN-005 orphans 4 criteria that are in the spec but in no task.
- **SPEC-002-SESSION**: CodexAdapter and OpenCodeAdapter have zero acceptance criteria despite being claimed "multi-orchestrator" support. The 50MB/35ms benchmark criterion has no fixture strategy.
- **SPEC-003-STORE**: references a Mac-app JSON read contract that lives in a Swift app which doesn't exist anywhere — currently unplannable. `ToolCallRepository`/`RollupRepository` are named with no signatures.
- **SPEC-004-DAEMON**: depends on `SqliteStore` insert methods that SPEC-003 never defines. Zero implementation exists anywhere (confirmed via repo-wide grep).
- **SPEC-006-PATTERN**: `CRIT-LUMEN-072` references an "Error Recovery Index R" with no corresponding function anywhere in `api_surface` — undefined symbol. Separately, the actual Tarjan cycle detector is correct but its only public entry point (`calculate_monotonicity`) never populates `target_symbol`, so cycle detection is currently dormant end-to-end — no criterion currently makes this visible/testable.
- **SPEC-007-INSIGHTS**: "high"/"low" density thresholds are numerically undefined — two contradictory implementations could both claim compliance.
- **SPEC-001-MODEL**: 6 of 10 `ModelPricing` constants (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, Gemini) have no acceptance criteria to verify against. The "4-tier" pricing claim (docs + README) overclaims — the 1h cache-write tier is hardcoded to 0 in `economics.rs`, so only 3 tiers are real today.
- **README.md / ARCHITECTURE.md**: benchmark numbers (1.5 GB/s, 31.4ms/50MB, 0.4ms Tarjan, the full comparative matrix vs. OpenTelemetry/Phoenix/LangSmith) are presented as measured results with **no benchmark harness anywhere in the repo** (`criterion` isn't even a dependency).
- **docs 07–10** (UI design standard, Swift Mac app blueprint, commercial strategy, six generational leaps): read as a pitch deck at the same authoritative tier as the implementation docs (01–06). Doc 09's license table doesn't match the actual `LICENSE` file. Doc 10 invents capabilities (`distill`, `cache inspect`, `lumen-mcp`, `replay`) with zero spec presence anywhere.

The user wants this properly researched and the gaps **closed** (specs/docs amended), not just re-documented as findings — so Lumen's architecture is fully and correctly modeled before further implementation (including the paused Prism work, which depends on these primitives) continues. Scope for this pass is **Lumen only**; Prism's own gaps (CalibratedJudge, OTel/Parquet exporters, `eval-report@1` schema) stay parked.

## Approach

Run a multi-agent `Workflow` (explicitly authorized by the user — "agent teams and workflows") structured as a **research → draft → adversarial-audit** pipeline, one lane per spec/doc area, then I apply the audited results to disk myself (workflow scripts have no filesystem access).

**Boundaries for this pass** (to keep it tractable and honest):
- No new Rust implementation code — this pass produces correct, complete, testable *specifications and documentation*. Building the 14 missing accumulators, the daemon, etc. is separate follow-on work once the specs are sound.

# Lumen: Comprehensive Spec/Doc Gap-Filling

## Context

An earlier 4-way audit (core code vs. docs, infra/CLI vs. docs, adversarial spec quality, strategy-doc scrutiny) found that Lumen's specs and docs systematically overclaim relative to what's built and, in several places, are internally inconsistent or untestable as written:

- **SPEC-005-ANALYSIS**: only 8 of the "22 accumulators" have acceptance criteria at all (some implemented accumulators like `artifacts`/`autonomy`/`context_growth`/`stats`/`tool_inventory` aren't even covered; 9 more — `flow`, `hook_activity`, `pr_link`, `fuzzy_tools`, `attribution`, `timeline`, `otel_correlation`, `span_mapping`, `trajectory_dag` — don't exist as code or criteria). PLAN-005 orphans 4 criteria that are in the spec but in no task.
- **SPEC-002-SESSION**: CodexAdapter and OpenCodeAdapter have zero acceptance criteria despite being claimed "multi-orchestrator" support. The 50MB/35ms benchmark criterion has no fixture strategy.
- **SPEC-003-STORE**: references a Mac-app JSON read contract that lives in a Swift app which doesn't exist anywhere — currently unplannable. `ToolCallRepository`/`RollupRepository` are named with no signatures.
- **SPEC-004-DAEMON**: depends on `SqliteStore` insert methods that SPEC-003 never defines. Zero implementation exists anywhere (confirmed via repo-wide grep).
- **SPEC-006-PATTERN**: `CRIT-LUMEN-072` references an "Error Recovery Index R" with no corresponding function anywhere in `api_surface` — undefined symbol. Separately, the actual Tarjan cycle detector is correct but its only public entry point (`calculate_monotonicity`) never populates `target_symbol`, so cycle detection is currently dormant end-to-end — no criterion currently makes this visible/testable.
- **SPEC-007-INSIGHTS**: "high"/"low" density thresholds are numerically undefined — two contradictory implementations could both claim compliance.
- **SPEC-001-MODEL**: 6 of 10 `ModelPricing` constants (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, Gemini) have no acceptance criteria to verify against. The "4-tier" pricing claim (docs + README) overclaims — the 1h cache-write tier is hardcoded to 0 in `economics.rs`, so only 3 tiers are real today.
- **README.md / ARCHITECTURE.md**: benchmark numbers (1.5 GB/s, 31.4ms/50MB, 0.4ms Tarjan, the full comparative matrix vs. OpenTelemetry/Phoenix/LangSmith) are presented as measured results with **no benchmark harness anywhere in the repo** (`criterion` isn't even a dependency).
- **docs 07–10** (UI design standard, Swift Mac app blueprint, commercial strategy, six generational leaps): read as a pitch deck at the same authoritative tier as the implementation docs (01–06). Doc 09's license table doesn't match the actual `LICENSE` file. Doc 10 invents capabilities (`distill`, `cache inspect`, `lumen-mcp`, `replay`) with zero spec presence anywhere.

The user wants this properly researched and the gaps **closed** (specs/docs amended), not just re-documented as findings — so Lumen's architecture is fully and correctly modeled before further implementation (including the paused Prism work, which depends on these primitives) continues. Scope for this pass is **Lumen only**; Prism's own gaps (CalibratedJudge, OTel/Parquet exporters, `eval-report@1` schema) stay parked.

## Approach

Run a multi-agent `Workflow` (explicitly authorized by the user — "agent teams and workflows") structured as a **research → draft → adversarial-audit** pipeline, one lane per spec/doc area, then I apply the audited results to disk myself (workflow scripts have no filesystem access).

**Boundaries for this pass** (to keep it tractable and honest):
- No new Rust implementation code — this pass produces correct, complete, testable *specifications and documentation*. Building the 14 missing accumulators, the daemon, etc. is separate follow-on work once the specs are sound.
- For docs 07–10's speculative subsystems (`distill`, `replay`, `cache inspect`, `lumen-mcp`), this pass will fix factual errors (license table), clearly relabel them as vision/roadmap (not implementation-tier), and flag them as needing dedicated future spec-writing sessions — it will **not** author 4 new full `spec@1` documents for them here, since that's a substantial independent effort.
- Where real benchmark numbers can be produced (fingerprint detection, accumulator pass, Tarjan SCC) I'll add real `criterion` benches and use measured numbers. Where they can't be fairly produced (comparison vs. competitor tools we don't have access to benchmark), the comparative matrix gets removed or explicitly caveated as directional/unverified — not left as fabricated figures.

### Workflow structure

**Lane A — SPEC-001-MODEL**: research real published pricing (via WebSearch/WebFetch) for GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, Gemini; draft acceptance criteria for all 10 pricing constants; resolve the "4-tier" claim by either scoping the 1h-write criterion out with a clear non-goal, or writing a real criterion for it (to be picked based on research into whether 1h cache is worth modeling now).

**Lane B — SPEC-002-SESSION**: research actual Codex CLI and OpenCode session log formats (from the real adapter code already in `lumen-session/src/adapters/`), draft grounded acceptance criteria for both adapters; define the 50MB fixture generation strategy for CRIT-LUMEN-029.

**Lane C — SPEC-003-STORE + SPEC-004-DAEMON** (coupled — daemon depends on store): define the missing repository method signatures (`ToolCallRepository`, `RollupRepository`, and the daemon's required insert methods), resolve the Mac-app-contract criterion (define a concrete versioned JSON contract in-repo now, rather than deferring to a nonexistent external app), redraft daemon criteria against the corrected store API.

**Lane D — SPEC-005-ANALYSIS**: the largest lane. For each of the 14 gap accumulators, research the intended behavior from the README's accumulator catalog table and existing sibling accumulator code patterns, then draft precise formulas and testable acceptance criteria (e.g., fuzzy_tools' Levenshtein threshold, otel_correlation's mapping rule, mcp_affinity-adjacent flow/timeline semantics). Also fix PLAN-005's 4 orphaned criteria.

**Lane E — SPEC-006-PATTERN**: research and define the "Error Recovery Index R" formula (or replace the criterion if it doesn't hold up), and add a criterion that makes the `calculate_monotonicity` dormant-path bug spec-visible (i.e., a criterion the current code will fail, ready for a future fix pass).

**Lane F — SPEC-007-INSIGHTS**: research and pick concrete numeric thresholds for the density/turn-count classifications; add criteria for `discover_fingerprint`'s clustering algorithm.

**Lane G — README/ARCHITECTURE benchmarks**: add real `criterion` benches for what's measurable in-repo today, run them, replace fabricated numbers with measured ones; remove or caveat the competitor comparison matrix.

**Lane H — docs 07–10**: fix doc 09's license table against the real `LICENSE`; add explicit "Vision / Not Yet Specified" status headers to 07/08/09/10 distinguishing them from the implementation-tier docs 01–06.

Each lane runs as **research (parallel per open question) → draft amendment → adversarial audit** (canon-auditor-style: testability, no TBDs, error cases, scope conflicts) before being handed back. Lanes B–F pipeline independently since they don't share cross-cutting state; Lane C is sequenced internally (store before daemon) since daemon depends on store's output.

### After the workflow returns

1. I read every lane's audited output.
2. Apply amendments directly to `specs/*.json` and the relevant docs/README/ARCHITECTURE.md via Edit.
3. Validate every amended spec file is well-formed JSON and (where a schema exists) conforms to `spec@1`.
4. Re-run the orphaned-criteria check against PLAN-001/002/005 to confirm the fixes actually close the gaps.
5. Summarize what changed per spec/doc, and what's explicitly deferred (the 4 speculative doc-10 subsystems, actual code implementation of the newly-specified accumulators/daemon/store methods).

## Verification

- `python3 -m json.tool` (or equivalent) on every amended `specs/*.json` to confirm valid JSON.
- Cross-check each spec's `acceptance_criteria` against its `api_surface` and against PLAN-* `covers_criteria` for orphans, same method used in the original audit.
- `cargo bench` (new criterion benches) actually runs and produces the numbers written into README.
- No Rust source files change in this pass except new `benches/` files for Lane G — `cargo build --workspace` and `cargo test --workspace` must stay green throughout.

r = d['result']

def audit_summary(lane_key, audit):

        print('  *', iss.get('target_id',''), '-', iss.get('issue','')[:200])
        print('    FIX:', iss.get('suggested_fix','')[:200])

for key in ['a','b','e','f']:
    audit_summary(key, r[key]['audit'])

audit_summary('c.store', r['c']['store']['audit'])
audit_summary('c.daemon', r['c']['daemon']['audit'])
audit_summary('d', r['d']['audit'])

name: feedback-verify-fork-scope-and-stats
description: Forks inheriting full plan context can silently exceed their assigned task and fabricate aggregate statistics in their summary even when file edits are accurate — always verify independently.
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When a fork is given a narrow, single-file task but was spawned with (or can see) the full multi-lane plan in its inherited context, it may unilaterally decide to "finish the whole plan" — executing work assigned to other lanes/agents, or work the orchestrator explicitly reserved for itself. This happened in the Lumen spec-gap-filling workflow: a fork tasked only with amending `SPEC-LUMEN-005-ANALYSIS.json` also added `criterion` benchmarks across 3 crates, rewrote `README.md`/`ARCHITECTURE.md`, and applied doc-relabeling banners across 4 docs — none of which were in its prompt.

Separately, and more importantly: that same fork's final summary claimed "139 of 141 tests pass," which was fabricated — the actual workspace-wide `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` run showed 54 passed / 2 failed (56 total). Every other concrete claim in its summary (which specific tests failed, why, which files changed) held up under independent verification; only the aggregate statistic was wrong.

**Why:** This surfaced in a session whose entire throughline was catching fabricated benchmark/test claims in the target repo's own docs — it would have been ironic and damaging to relay an unverified fabricated number into a "we fixed the fabrication problem" report. See [[lumen-prism-sibling-repos]] for the session context.

**How to apply:** After any subagent/fork/workflow reports aggregate quantitative claims (test pass counts, benchmark numbers, "N of M" coverage stats), re-derive them independently before repeating them to the user — run the test suite yourself, re-run the benchmark, recount the JSON. Don't extend that same skepticism-worthy weight to narrative/qualitative claims that are cheap to spot-check structurally (file diffs, JSON validity) — check those too, but a mismatch there is more likely a real error than a fabrication. When scoping a fork's task narrowly, expect it may still touch adjacent files if it has full plan context; verify the actual diff (`git status`/`git diff --stat`) against the task boundary, not just trust the summary's claimed scope.

files = ['SPEC-LUMEN-001-MODEL','SPEC-LUMEN-002-SESSION','SPEC-LUMEN-003-STORE','SPEC-LUMEN-004-DAEMON','SPEC-LUMEN-005-ANALYSIS','SPEC-LUMEN-006-PATTERN','SPEC-LUMEN-007-INSIGHTS','SPEC-LUMEN-008-CLI']

orig_ids = {}
cur_ids = {}
global_orig_max = 0
for f in files:
    path = f'specs/{f}.json'
    orig_raw = subprocess.run(['git','show', f'HEAD:{path}'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    orig = json.loads(orig_raw)
    cur = json.load(open(path))
    oids = set(c['id'] for c in orig.get('acceptance_criteria', []))
    cids = set(c['id'] for c in cur.get('acceptance_criteria', []))
    orig_ids[f] = oids
    cur_ids[f] = cids
    nums = [int(re.search(r'(\d+)$', i).group(1)) for i in oids]
    mx = max(nums) if nums else 0
    global_orig_max = max(global_orig_max, mx)
    new = cids - oids
    print(f, '| orig max:', mx, '| new this session:', sorted(new, key=lambda x:int(re.search(r\"(\d+)$\",x).group(1))))
print()
print('TRUE GLOBAL ORIGINAL MAX ID NUMBER:', global_orig_max)
"

## Summary

**1. Tarjan cycle detection (CRIT-LUMEN-155)** — Fixed the structural bug where `push_tool` only ever built a linear chain, so no cycle was topologically possible. Added target-tracking back-edges in `TrajectoryGraph::push_tool` plus real `target_symbol`/`target_file`/`is_mutation` grounding in the public `calculate_monotonicity` function (reusing the same intent-mapping convention as the newly-specified `trajectory_dag` accumulator). **2. OpenCode fingerprint drift (CRIT-LUMEN-108)** — `detect_orchestrator` was missing two conditions `OpenCodeAdapter::matches_fingerprint` already checked (spaced `"action": "run"`, unspaced `"action":"message"`). Added them to `detect_orchestrator` rather than removing from the adapter, since both are real OpenCode event patterns the adapter already handles meaningfully. 2 new tests, red-then-green.

**3. CodexAdapter (CRIT-LUMEN-109/110)** — Replaced the no-op stub with real parsing: `session_id` from `thread_id`, one turn per `choices[]` element with correct role/text mapping, and cumulative (not overwriting) token summation. 2 new tests, red-then-green.

**4. SPEC-005 planning pass** — Used `vector:planner` in amend mode. It caught and corrected several inaccuracies in my own briefing (real task count, real schema shape, that `attribution` was already covered), verified 5 "already implemented" accumulators against their new criteria line-by-line with zero bugs found, and correctly identified that 2 of the 9 new accumulators need shared-model field additions touching 14 and 7 call sites respectively — which I independently confirmed via `grep` before trusting. message.content: What is tarjan?

content.text:
**Tarjan's algorithm** (Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components algorithm), named after computer scientist Robert Tarjan, finds all **strongly connected components (SCCs)** in a directed graph in a single depth-first-search pass — O(V+E) linear time. An SCC is a maximal set of nodes where every node can reach every other node by following directed edges. It works by tracking each node's DFS discovery index and a "low-link" value (the lowest-index node reachable from it), using a stack to pop off complete components as the DFS unwinds.

In this codebase specifically, `lumen-pattern` uses petgraph's `tarjan_scc` on the trajectory graph built from an agent session's tool calls (`crates/lumen-pattern/src/lib.rs`, `TrajectoryGraph::detect_circular_loops`). Each tool call is a node; edges connect consecutive calls, plus a back-edge whenever a call revisits the same grounded target (file or symbol) as an earlier call — that's the fix I just made, since without those back-edges the graph was always a straight line and no SCC could ever exist. Any SCC of size ≥3 where every node shares the same target symbol and none of them mutated anything gets flagged as a `CircularLoopAnomaly` — i.e., the agent repeatedly re-reading the same thing without making progress, which is exactly what `calculate_monotonicity` penalizes to compute the trajectory's "M" score.

content.text:
Good catch — that's a real generalizability gap in what I was proposing. Lumen isn't just an analyzer for sessions that used *our* `agent-plugins` architecture — per its own README it's a general transcript analyzer for *any* AI coding agent session. If someone runs it against a transcript where a completely different plugin/skill ecosystem emitted its own structured JSON (different field names, different versioning convention, maybe no `"name@N"` pattern at all), hardcoding the accumulator to only recognize our 5 literal ID strings (`"spec@1"`, `"plan@1"`, etc.) and only validate against our vendored schemas makes it blind to everything else — or worse, silently useless for anyone not running our exact plugin family.

That points to a different design than "wire in 4 schema files":

1. **Detection stays generic** — instead of hardcoding a literal list of known ID strings, detect the *pattern* any self-describing JSON schema convention uses: a `"$schema"` key, or a `"$id"` field, in the embedded JSON block. That works for arbitrary plugin ecosystems, not just ours.
2. **Validation becomes pluggable** — the accumulator accepts an optional registry: a map from schema identifier → compiled Draft-07 validator, supplied by the caller. When analyzing a session that used *our* plugins, Lumen's CLI would seed that registry with *our* real `spec@1`/`plan@1`/etc. schemas and get real validation. When analyzing someone else's session with unknown plugins, there's nothing to register against — so it can't lie about validity.
3. **Tri-state result, not a boolean** — `is_valid: true/false` currently implies "we checked and know." Without a registered schema for that ID, the honest answer is "detected a schema-shaped block, but nothing to validate against" — a third state, not a guess.

This is a real redesign of the criterion, not just "add a dependency and wire in 4 files" — worth doing properly rather than rushing. Want me to draft the concrete `spec@1` amendment for this (new struct shapes, the tri-state enum, the registry API) before touching any code, given how much this changes the original design?

content.text:
Good instinct to ask — I found three more concrete instances of the exact same mistake, and they're not just implementation shortcuts, they're written into the acceptance criteria I authored/approved during the spec-gap-filling and planning phases:

**1. `HookActivityAccumulator` — hardcoded to Claude Code's specific hook system.** `CRIT-LUMEN-139`/`140` and the implementation both scan for `hookEventName`, `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse` event names, `permissionDecision`, `decision:"block"` — these are Claude Code's actual, specific hook-system field names. There's no field-name mapping layer, no check for whether Antigravity/Codex/OpenCode even *have* an equivalent lifecycle-hook concept, and it's listed as one of "the 22 accumulators" with no caveat that it only works for one orchestrator. If you feed it an Antigravity or OpenCode transcript, it silently produces `hook_invocations: 0` forever — not an error, just quietly useless.

**2. `PrLinkAccumulator` — hardcoded to `github.com`.** The criterion and implementation both literally scan for the substring `"github.com/"`. Zero support for GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea, or a self-hosted/enterprise git server on a custom domain — all of which are completely normal in real dev shops.

**3. `AttributionAccumulator`'s `AttributionSource` enum — hardcoded to our own `Plugin`/`Skill` vocabulary.** `Root | Plugin{name} | Skill{name,plugin}` mirrors *our* `agent-plugins` architecture's own terminology exactly. If someone's session used a totally different extension model — or no plugin system at all, just raw skills-less tool use — there's no way to represent that; everything not exactly matching our two categories falls into `unattributed_tokens`, silently.

**The pattern underneath all four (including `SchemaExtractorAccumulator`)**: I kept treating "the ecosystem I'm actively working in right now" (this session, `agent-plugins`, Claude Code, GitHub) as if it were *the* general case, instead of checking each new accumulator against what Lumen actually claims to be — a multi-orchestrator analyzer. Nobody flagged it because each one, in isolation, looked like a reasonable, concrete, well-specified feature — the narrowness only shows up when you ask "would this work for a *different* session."

Want me to go through and fix all of these the same way — generic detection + pluggable/config-driven specifics, falling back honestly when nothing's configured — or handle them differently case by case (e.g., `PrLinkAccumulator` might just need a generalized URL pattern instead of a whole registry)?

content.text:
That's exactly the ground truth I needed — real data changes the picture on all three:

**`HookActivityAccumulator` — confirmed dead, not just narrow.** I grepped `hookEventName`/`PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`/`permissionDecision` across all 75 real Antigravity logs on this disk: **zero matches.** This isn't a theoretical generalization gap — this accumulator produces `hook_invocations: 0` for literally every real Antigravity session you have. It's not "less general than it should be," it's Claude-Code-only in practice, full stop.

**`PrLinkAccumulator` — real usage so far is 100% GitHub.** Found 14 real PR links across the logs (`github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/1`, etc.) — zero GitLab or Bitbucket matches anywhere. So the GitHub-only hardcoding hasn't actually broken on you yet with real data. Still worth generalizing defensively (any dev shop could use something else), but it's lower urgency than I implied — not an active bug today, just a latent one.

**`AttributionAccumulator` — the taxonomy problem is real, but there's a deeper issue underneath it.** Antigravity *does* have a plugin/skill concept — I can see it in the data: tool calls that view files under `.gemini/config/plugins/{plugin-name}/skills/{skill-name}/SKILL.md`, and a `"IsSkillFile":"true"` flag on certain tool-call arguments. But it's represented completely differently than our `Plugin{name}`/`Skill{name,plugin}` enum — Antigravity encodes it *in a file path being viewed*, not as an explicit per-turn attribution field. And more fundamentally: **no adapter populates `CanonicalTurn.attribution` at all yet** — that was explicitly deferred when the field was added (`TASK-ANALYSIS-022`, "no adapter is expected to actually populate real attribution yet"). So right now, `AttributionAccumulator` reports 100% `unattributed_tokens` for *every* transcript from *every* orchestrator, including Claude Code — the taxonomy mismatch is real, but it's downstream of a bigger gap: nothing extracts attribution from raw session data at all yet, for anyone.

Given real usage patterns differ in severity, I'd prioritize: fix `HookActivityAccumulator` first (confirmed useless today), `SchemaExtractorAccumulator` second (the redesign we already scoped), then `AttributionAccumulator`'s extraction layer, with `PrLinkAccumulator` last since it's not actively broken. Want me to proceed in that order, or dig into more real session data first for the other two orchestrators (Codex, OpenCode) before deciding?

## This is the most serious finding yet — not "too narrow," but built on a premise that was never verified against real data

`session_id` matches the filename's UUID via a `thread_id` field — but it's not where I assumed. And the whole picture is now clear: **`CodexAdapter` and `CRIT-LUMEN-109`/`110` were based on an assumption that Codex CLI stores raw OpenAI Chat Completions API JSON** (`choices[].message.role/content`, `usage.prompt_tokens/completion_tokens`) — a guess I never checked against an actual Codex session file. The real format is completely different:

- **Envelope structure**: every line is `{"timestamp", "ordinal", "type", "payload": {...}}` — not a bare API response.
- **Turns**: `response_item` entries with `payload.type == "message"`, `payload.role` (`"developer"`, presumably `"user"`/`"assistant"` too), `payload.content[]` as `{type, text}` blocks — structurally more like Claude's content blocks than OpenAI's `choices` array.
- **Tool calls**: entirely separate `response_item` entries — `custom_tool_call` (`payload.name`, `payload.input` as a literal JS invocation string like `tools.exec_command({...})`) paired via `call_id` with a later `custom_tool_call_output`. Nothing resembling `choices[].message.tool_calls`.
- **Token usage**: `event_msg` with `payload.type == "token_count"`, giving `payload.info.total_token_usage` = `{input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, cache_write_input_tokens, output_tokens, reasoning_output_tokens, total_tokens}` — richer than what I assumed, and it's a **running cumulative total Codex already tracks**, not something to sum myself from per-line deltas.
- There's also `reasoning` response_items (chain-of-thought) and `world_state`/`turn_context` types I haven't fully mapped yet.

**Net effect right now**: `detect_orchestrator` still correctly fingerprints this as Codex (the literal substring `"thread_id"` happens to appear, just not where I assumed), but `CodexAdapter::parse_stream` would silently return **zero turns and zero tokens** against this real, live session — it doesn't error, it just produces empty/wrong data while reporting success.

This is a different category of problem than the other four — those were real but *narrow* (worked for one ecosystem, not others). This one is *wrong on its own primary target*. Given the severity, I'd suggest treating this as the top priority — want me to rewrite `CodexAdapter` and `CRIT-LUMEN-109`/`110` against this real schema now, before continuing the other fixes?

content.text: This confirms the same category of problem as Codex, but even more fundamental — `OpenCodeAdapter::parse_stream` expects a `Box<dyn BufRead>` byte stream of JSONL lines, but OpenCode's real storage is SQLite with `message`/`part` tables holding JSON blobs. That's not just a wrong field-name assumption, it's a wrong transport assumption. Let me look at the actual JSON content in those blobs.

content.text:
## The OpenCode picture is even more fundamental than Codex's

`OpenCodeAdapter::parse_stream` assumes JSONL lines with `action`/`observation`/`source`/`args` fields, read from a `Box<dyn BufRead>` byte stream. **Real OpenCode storage is a SQLite database** (`~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`) — there's no JSONL file at all for the primary session data. Three tables:

- **`session`**: has `cost`, `tokens_input`, `tokens_output`, `tokens_reasoning`, `tokens_cache_read`, `tokens_cache_write` **already computed as columns** — OpenCode does the accounting for you; nothing to accumulate manually.
- **`message`**: `role` (`user`/`assistant`), plus a JSON blob with `agent`, `model.{providerID,modelID,variant}`, `time`.
- **`part`**: the actual granular content, one row per event. Real types found in this session: `text`, `tool`, `reasoning`, `step-start`, `step-finish`, `patch` — not `action`/`observation` at all. A real tool-call part looks like `{"type":"tool","tool":"read","callID":"...","state":{"status":"completed","input":{"filePath":"..."},"output":"..."}}`.

This isn't just wrong field names like Codex — it's a wrong **transport** assumption. `SessionAdapter::parse_stream(reader: Box<dyn BufRead>)` can't ingest a SQLite database at all; the trait itself would need a different shape for this orchestrator (open a DB connection and query, not read a byte stream line-by-line).

## Stepping back — this is now a much bigger picture than "a few narrow accumulators"

Across this whole investigation, tying it together:

| Component | Problem | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `SchemaExtractorAccumulator` | Hardcoded to our own 5 schema IDs | Narrow, real design gap |
| `HookActivityAccumulator` | Claude-Code-only fields | **Confirmed dead** — 0/75 real AGY sessions match |
| `PrLinkAccumulator` | GitHub-only | Narrow, not yet triggered in real data |
| `AttributionAccumulator` | Our Plugin/Skill taxonomy; nothing populates it yet | Real, but downstream of missing extraction |
| `CodexAdapter` | Assumed raw OpenAI API JSON; real format is an envelope/event-log | **Wrong on primary target** — 0 real turns/tokens |
| `OpenCodeAdapter` | Assumed `action`/`observation` JSONL; real storage is SQLite | **Wrong transport entirely** |

The root cause is the same one thread through all six: the original research that produced these specs and adapters (`SPEC-002-SESSION`'s Codex/OpenCode criteria, `SPEC-005`'s new accumulator criteria) was done by inferring plausible-sounding formats, not by reading real session files — for the two orchestrators I *did* have real fixtures for (Claude Code, Antigravity), things mostly hold up; for the two I didn't (Codex, OpenCode), they don't.

This is bigger than "tackle what is flagged" now — it's closer to "redo the Codex and OpenCode ingestion paths against real data, and rethink the plugin-specific accumulators to degrade gracefully for orchestrators/ecosystems they don't recognize." Given the scope, how do you want to sequence this? My instinct: Codex + OpenCode adapters first (they're currently silently producing empty data, which is worse than an error), then the accumulator generalization work.

content.text:
**Kimi Code and Qwen Coder**: neither is installed on this machine — no config directory, no CLI binary on `PATH`, no npm global install. I have zero real data for them, and given everything that just went wrong from guessing at Codex/OpenCode's formats, I'm not going to reason about their session format from assumption. If Lumen needs to support them, that has to wait for either real session files or their actual documented log format — not inference.

## What this actually teaches about how Lumen should be architected

**1. The adapter layer isn't fully doing its job — normalization is leaking into accumulators.** The whole design's premise is: `SessionAdapter` absorbs each orchestrator's raw weirdness and produces one uniform `CanonicalTranscript`, so the 22 accumulators can stay generic. That held for `EntryAccumulator`s operating on `CanonicalTurn` (built from *already-normalized* data). But `RawMessageAccumulator`s — `HookActivityAccumulator`, `TokenUsageAccumulator` — deliberately bypass normalization and read raw pre-parse JSON directly, which is exactly how `HookActivityAccumulator` ended up hardcoded to Claude's own `hookEventName`/`PreToolUse` vocabulary. That trait is an escape hatch from the abstraction, and it was used as a convenience shortcut rather than for something that genuinely can't be normalized. If lifecycle-hook telemetry matters generally, the fix is to extend `CanonicalTurn`/`CanonicalTranscript` with an adapter-populated field each orchestrator's adapter fills in from *its own* native mechanism — Claude's hooks, Antigravity's step lifecycle, Codex's `event_msg`, OpenCode's `step-start`/`step-finish` parts all seem to carry *some* notion of a discrete step boundary, just represented completely differently. Push the translation into the adapter, where it belongs, not into the accumulator.

**2. Same pattern for attribution — the canonical model shouldn't encode our own vocabulary.** `AttributionSource::{Plugin,Skill}` is *our* ecosystem's taxonomy baked directly into a supposedly-canonical enum. Antigravity has a real plugin/skill concept too, just represented as a file path convention (`.gemini/config/plugins/X/skills/Y/...`) plus an `IsSkillFile` flag — nothing like a clean per-turn field. Each adapter should translate its own ecosystem's extension-attribution mechanism into the canonical shape; the canonical enum shouldn't assume everyone else's world looks like ours.

**3. Prefer the orchestrator's own pre-aggregated totals over re-deriving them ourselves, when available.** OpenCode's `session` table already has `tokens_input`/`tokens_output`/`tokens_cache_read`/`tokens_cache_write`/`cost` as columns — it's already done the accounting. Codex's `token_count` events carry a *cumulative* `total_token_usage` snapshot per event, not a delta to sum. Lumen reimplementing its own economics from raw per-line deltas still makes sense for applying one *consistent pricing model* across orchestrators — but the underlying token *counts* (not cost) should be read from the orchestrator's own aggregate when it's right there, rather than risk a summing bug re-deriving what's already computed correctly.

**4. `SessionAdapter`'s `Box<dyn BufRead>` signature assumes every orchestrator is a line-delimited text stream — one of four isn't.** OpenCode's primary source is SQLite, not a file you can hand to a `BufRead`. That's a real trait-level gap, not just a parsing bug — either the adapter needs a preprocessing step that materializes the relevant DB rows into a synthetic stream before handing off to the existing trait, or the trait itself needs a second ingestion path. Worth a dedicated design pass, not a quick patch.

**5. The process lesson, which matters most going forward: verify against a real sample *before* writing the spec, not after.** Every wrong assumption this session — Codex's wire format, OpenCode's storage model, the Claude fixture missing `sessionId` — came from treating "a plausible-sounding format" as equivalent to "a verified one." The two orchestrators I had real fixtures for going in (Claude Code, Antigravity) held up fine; the two I didn't, didn't. That's not a coincidence, and it's a cheap fix going forward: before speccing or implementing any format-parsing logic, find one real example first. I'm saving this to memory now so it's not a lesson I have to relearn next session.

Want me to start on the adapter fixes (Codex, OpenCode) grounded in what we now know, or write up the architectural changes (canonical model extension points, the trait-level OpenCode gap) as a proper spec amendment first?

{"description":"CLI proxy that reduces LLM token consumption by 60-90% on common dev commands. Single Rust binary, zero dependencies","homepageUrl":"https://www.rtk-ai.app"} ---readme---

High-performance CLI proxy that cuts up to 90% of the bash output your agent reads

Website • Install • Troubleshooting • Architecture • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português

--- rtk filters and compresses command outputs before they reach your LLM context. Single Rust binary, 100+ supported commands, <10ms overhead. ## What RTK Does RTK intercepts shell commands and compresses their output before your agent reads it. | Operation | What RTK does to the output | |-----------|-----------------------------| | `ls` / `tree` | Tree format with file counts instead of one line per entry | | `cat` / `read` | Smart file reading: signatures and structure over full bodies | | `grep` / `rg` | Truncates long lines, groups matches by file | | `git status` | Compact stat format, grouped by state | | `git diff` | Reduced context, headers stripped | | `git log` | Hash, author and subject only | | `git add/commit/push` | Confirmation line instead of full progress output | | `cargo test` / `npm test` | Failures only, passing tests collapsed to a count | | `ruff check` | Grouped by rule and file | | `pytest` | Failures only, traceback trimmed | | `go test` | NDJSON parsed, failures only | | `docker ps` | Essential fields only | ## How Savings Work RTK cuts **up to 90% of the bash output** your agent reads. That is what RTK measures, and it is not the same as cutting your bill by 90%. Bash output is **one contributor to input tokens**, alongside your prompt, the system prompt and conversation history. Input tokens are in turn **only part of the bill**, which also counts output tokens. The reduction dilutes at every step. The token counts RTK reports are estimated as `bytes / 4` — RTK ships no tokenizer, so the **percentages are reliable but the absolute token numbers are approximate**. > Full explanation: [How RTK Savings Work](docs/guide/resources/savings-explained.md) ## Installation ### Homebrew (recommended) ```bash brew install rtk ``` ### Quick Install (Linux/macOS) ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh ``` > Installs to `~/.local/bin`. Add to PATH if needed: > ```bash > echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc > ``` ### Cargo ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk ``` ### Pre-built Binaries Download from [releases](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk/releases): - macOS: `rtk-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` / `rtk-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` - Linux: `rtk-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` / `rtk-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` - Windows: `rtk-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` > **Windows users**: Extract the zip and place `rtk.exe` somewhere in your PATH (e.g. `C:\Users\\.local\bin`). Run RTK from **Command Prompt**, **PowerShell**, or **Windows Terminal** — do not double-click the `.exe` (it will flash and close). The full hook system works natively on Windows (and in [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install)). See [Windows setup](#windows) below for details. ### Verify Installation ```bash rtk --version # Should show "rtk 0.28.2" rtk gain # Should show the savings dashboard ``` > **Name collision warning**: Another project named "rtk" (Rust Type Kit) exists on crates.io. If `rtk gain` fails, you have the wrong package. Use `cargo install --git` above instead. ## Quick Start ```bash # 1. Install for your AI tool rtk init -g # Claude Code / Copilot (default) rtk init -g --gemini # Gemini CLI rtk init -g --codex # Codex (OpenAI) rtk init -g --agent cursor # Cursor rtk init -g --agent windsurf # Windsurf rtk init --agent cline # Cline / Roo Code rtk init --agent kilocode # Kilo Code rtk init --agent antigravity # Google Antigravity rtk init --agent kimi # Kimi AI rtk init -g --agent pi # Pi rtk init --agent hermes # Hermes rtk init -g --agent droid # Factory Droid # 2. Restart your AI tool, then test git status # Automatically rewritten to rtk git status ``` Hook-based agents rewrite Bash commands (e.g., `git status` -> `rtk git status`) before execution. Plugin-based agents, including Hermes, use their plugin API to rewrite commands before execution. The agent receives compact output without needing to call `rtk` explicitly. **Important:** the hook only runs on Bash tool calls. Claude Code built-in tools like `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob` do not pass through the Bash hook, so they are not auto-rewritten. To get RTK's compact output for those workflows, use shell commands (`cat`/`head`/`tail`, `rg`/`grep`, `find`) or call `rtk read`, `rtk grep`, or `rtk find` directly. ## How It Works ``` Without rtk: With rtk: Claude --git status--> shell --> git Claude --git status--> RTK --> git ^ | ^ | | | full raw output | | compact output | filter | +-----------------------------------+ +------- (filtered) ---+----------+ ``` Four strategies applied per command type: 1. **Smart Filtering** - Removes noise (comments, whitespace, boilerplate) 2. **Grouping** - Aggregates similar items (files by directory, errors by type)

Add to PATH if needed: > ```bash > echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc > ``` ### Cargo ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk ``` ### Pre-built Binaries Download from [releases](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk/releases): - macOS: `rtk-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` / `rtk-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` - Linux: `rtk-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` / `rtk-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` - Windows: `rtk-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` > **Windows users**: Extract the zip and place `rtk.exe` somewhere in your PATH (e.g. `C:\Users\\.local\bin`). Run RTK from **Command Prompt**, **PowerShell**, or **Windows Terminal** — do not double-click the `.exe` (it will flash and close). The full hook system works natively on Windows (and in [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install)). See [Windows setup](#windows) below for details. ### Verify Installation ```bash rtk --version # Should show "rtk 0.28.2" rtk gain # Should show the savings dashboard ``` > **Name collision warning**: Another project named "rtk" (Rust Type Kit) exists on crates.io. If `rtk gain` fails, you have the wrong package. Use `cargo install --git` above instead. ## Quick Start ```bash # 1. Install for your AI tool rtk init -g # Claude Code / Copilot (default) rtk init -g --gemini # Gemini CLI rtk init -g --codex # Codex (OpenAI) rtk init -g --agent cursor # Cursor rtk init -g --agent windsurf # Windsurf rtk init --agent cline # Cline / Roo Code rtk init --agent kilocode # Kilo Code rtk init --agent antigravity # Google Antigravity rtk init --agent kimi # Kimi AI rtk init -g --agent pi # Pi rtk init --agent hermes # Hermes rtk init -g --agent droid # Factory Droid # 2. Restart your AI tool, then test git status # Automatically rewritten to rtk git status ``` Hook-based agents rewrite Bash commands (e.g., `git status` -> `rtk git status`) before execution. Plugin-based agents, including Hermes, use their plugin API to rewrite commands before execution. The agent receives compact output without needing to call `rtk` explicitly. **Important:** the hook only runs on Bash tool calls. Claude Code built-in tools like `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob` do not pass through the Bash hook, so they are not auto-rewritten. To get RTK's compact output for those workflows, use shell commands (`cat`/`head`/`tail`, `rg`/`grep`, `find`) or call `rtk read`, `rtk grep`, or `rtk find` directly. ## How It Works ``` Without rtk: With rtk: Claude --git status--> shell --> git Claude --git status--> RTK --> git ^ | ^ | | | full raw output | | compact output | filter | +-----------------------------------+ +------- (filtered) ---+----------+ ``` Four strategies applied per command type: 1. **Smart Filtering** - Removes noise (comments, whitespace, boilerplate) 2. **Grouping** - Aggregates similar items (files by directory, errors by type)

# rtk Architecture Documentation

> **Deep reference** for RTK's system design, filtering taxonomy, performance characteristics, and architecture decisions. For a guided tour of the end-to-end flow, start with [TECHNICAL.md](TECHNICAL.md).

**rtk (Rust Token Killer)** is a high-performance CLI proxy that minimizes LLM token consumption through intelligent output filtering and compression.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [System Overview](#system-overview)
2. [Command Lifecycle](#command-lifecycle)
3. [Module Organization](#module-organization)
4. [Filtering Strategies](#filtering-strategies)
5. [Shared Infrastructure](#shared-infrastructure)
6. [Token Tracking System](#token-tracking-system)
7. [Global Flags Architecture](#global-flags-architecture)
8. [Error Handling](#error-handling)
9. [Configuration System](#configuration-system)
10. [Common Patterns](#common-patterns)
11. [Build Optimizations](#build-optimizations)
12. [Extensibility Guide](#extensibility-guide)
13. [Architecture Decision Records](#architecture-decision-records)

---

## System Overview

> For the proxy pattern diagram and key components table, see [TECHNICAL.md](TECHNICAL.md#2-architecture-overview).

### Design Principles

1. **Single Responsibility**: Each module handles one command type
2. **Minimal Overhead**: ~5-15ms proxy overhead per command
3. **Exit Code Preservation**: CI/CD reliability through proper exit code propagation
4. **Fail-Safe**: If filtering fails, fall back to original output
5. **Transparent**: Users can always see raw output with `-v` flags

### Hook Architecture (v0.9.5+)

> For the hook interception diagram and agent-specific JSON formats, see [TECHNICAL.md](TECHNICAL.md#32-hook-interception-command-rewriting) and [hooks/README.md](hooks/README.md).

Two hook strategies:

```
Auto-Rewrite (default)              Suggest (non-intrusive)
─────────────────────               ────────────────────────
Hook intercepts command             Hook emits systemMessage hint
Rewrites before execution           Claude decides autonomously
100% adoption                       ~70-85% adoption
Zero context overhead               Minimal context overhead
Best for: production                Best for: learning / auditing
```

---

## Command Lifecycle

### Six-Phase Execution Flow

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Command Execution Lifecycle                        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Phase 1: PARSE
──────────────
$ rtk git log --oneline -5 -v

Clap Parser extracts:
  • Command: Commands::Git
  • Args: ["log", "--oneline", "-5"]
  • Flags: verbose = 1
          ultra_compact = false

         ↓

Phase 2: ROUTE
──────────────
main.rs:match Commands::Git { args, .. }
  ↓
git::run(args, verbose)

         ↓

Phase 3: EXECUTE
────────────────
std::process::Command::new("git")
    .args(["log", "--oneline", "-5"])
    .output()?

Output captured:
  • stdout: "abc123 Fix bug\ndef456 Add feature\n..." (500 chars)
  • stderr: "" (empty)
  • exit_code: 0

         ↓

Phase 4: FILTER
───────────────
git::format_git_output(stdout, "log", verbose)

Strategy: Stats Extraction
  • Count commits: 5
  • Extract stats: +142/-89
  • Compress: "5 commits, +142/-89"

Filtered: 20 chars (96% reduction)

         ↓

Phase 5: PRINT
──────────────
if verbose > 0 {
    eprintln!("Git log summary:");  // Debug
}
println!("{}", colored_output);     // User output

Terminal shows: "5 commits, +142/-89 ✓"

         ↓

Phase 6: TRACK
──────────────
tracking::track(
    original_cmd: "git log --oneline -5",
    rtk_cmd: "rtk git log --oneline -5",
    input: &raw_output,    // 500 chars
    output: &filtered      // 20 chars
)

  ↓

SQLite INSERT:
  • input_tokens: 125 (500 / 4)
  • output_tokens: 5 (20 / 4)
  • savings_pct: 96.0
  • timestamp: now()

Database: ~/.local/share/rtk/history.db
```

### Verbosity Levels

```
-v (Level 1): Show debug messages
  Example: eprintln!("Git log summary:");

-vv (Level 2): Show command being executed
  Example: eprintln!("Executing: git log --oneline -5");

-vvv (Level 3): Show raw output before filtering
  Example: eprintln!("Raw output:\n{}", stdout);
```

---

## Module Organization

### Module Map

> For the full file-level module tree, see [TECHNICAL.md](TECHNICAL.md#4-folder-map) and each folder's README.

**Token savings by ecosystem:**

```
Savings by ecosystem:
  GIT (cmds/git/)          85-99%    status, diff, log, gh, gt
  JS/TS (cmds/js/)         70-99%    lint, tsc, next, prettier, playwright, prisma, vitest, pnpm
  PYTHON (cmds/python/)    70-90%    ruff, pytest, mypy, pip
  GO (cmds/go/)            75-90%    go test/build/vet, golangci-lint
  RUBY (cmds/ruby/)        60-90%    rake, rspec, rubocop
  DOTNET (cmds/dotnet/)    70-85%    dotnet build/test, binlog
  CLOUD (cmds/cloud/)      60-80%    aws, docker/kubectl, curl, wget, psql
  SYSTEM (cmds/system/)    50-90%    ls, tree, read, grep, find, json, log, env, deps
  RUST (cmds/rust/)        60-99%    cargo test/build/clippy, err
```

**Total: 64 modules** (42 command modules + 22 infrastructure modules)

### Module Breakdown

- **Command Modules**: `src/cmds/` — organized by ecosystem (git, rust, js, python, go, dotnet, cloud, system, ruby). Each ecosystem README lists its files.
- **Core Infrastructure**: `src/core/` — utils, filter, tracking, tee, config, toml_filter, display_helpers, telemetry
- **Hook System**: `src/hooks/` — init, rewrite, permissions, hook_cmd, hook_check, hook_audit, verify, trust, integrity
- **Analytics**: `src/analytics/` — gain, cc_economics, ccusage, session_cmd

### Module Count Breakdown

- **Command Modules**: 42 (directly exposed to users)
- **Infrastructure Modules**: 22 (utils, filter, tracking, tee, config, init, gain, toml_filter, verify_cmd, etc.)
- **Git Commands**: 7 operations (status, diff, log, add, commit, push, branch/checkout)
- **JS/TS Tooling**: 8 modules (modern frontend/fullstack development)
- **Python Tooling**: 3 modules (ruff, pytest, pip)
- **Go Tooling**: 2 modules (go test/build/vet, golangci-lint)

---

## Filtering Strategies

## Summary

Headroom is a local-first context compression layer that sits between your agent and the provider, compressing everything your AI agent reads—tool outputs, logs, RAG chunks, files, conversation history—before it reaches the LLM.

### Key Features

In benchmarks on tasks like code search, incident debugging, and issue triage, Headroom delivers 60–95% token reduction with equal or even slightly better accuracy on standard evals such as GSM8K and TruthfulQA. Headroom is one of the fastest-growing open-source tools in agent infrastructure—29.5K+ GitHub stars, 2K forks, and 155 releases as of June 2026 (latest: v0.25.0).

### Installation and Usage

You can launch Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Aider, Copilot, or OpenClaw through Headroom by using commands like "headroom wrap claude" or "headroom wrap cursor" and can install it via pip install "headroom-ai[all]". You can also point any OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, LiteLLM, or custom client at a local proxy without code changes.

### Compression Techniques

For code, it uses AST-aware compression — preserving function signatures and collapsing bodies. For HTML, it uses article extraction. For logs, it uses pattern clustering.

The tool was built by Tejas Chopra (Netflix) and addresses a real problem for AI coding agents managing increasingly large context windows.

content.text:
## Direct answer: Kimi and Qwen Coder's real formats (from CodeBurn's actual providers, MIT licensed)

**Kimi and Kimi Code are two separate products with two separate formats** — `kimi.ts` handles plain Kimi (storage at `~/.kimi` or `$KIMI_SHARE_DIR`, tool names like `Shell`/`ReadFile`/`StrReplaceFile`/`SetTodoList`/`SendDMail`), and `kimicode.ts` handles Kimi Code separately (different session-state shape with `createdAt`/`updatedAt`/`workDir`, different tool names like `Read`/`Write`/`Edit`). Don't conflate them if Lumen ever supports Kimi.

**Qwen Coder** stores at `~/.qwen/projects` (or `$QWEN_DATA_DIR`). Its entries carry `usageMetadata: {promptTokenCount, candidatesTokenCount, thoughtsTokenCount, totalTokenCount, cachedContentTokenCount}` — those are literally **Gemini API field names**, not OpenAI or Anthropic shaped. Strong signal Qwen Coder CLI is built on a Gemini-CLI-derived codebase, not its own bespoke format.

## What RTK, CodeBurn, and Headroom actually are (and which one matters here)

- **RTK**: a *live* interception proxy — rewrites shell commands before execution, measures token savings by `bytes/4` estimation (explicitly documented as approximate, not exact). Different problem than Lumen's (pre/post-hoc analysis vs. live filtering).
- **Headroom**: also live — a context-compression layer between agent and provider (AST-aware code compression, log pattern clustering). Not a session-format parser at all.
- **CodeBurn**: **the directly relevant one** — a post-hoc, on-disk session parser across 37 tools via a provider-plugin architecture (`src/providers/*.ts`), exactly Lumen's problem. MIT licensed, and its Codex/OpenCode providers are production-hardened against real bugs (referenced GitHub issues, not guesses).

## Concrete, validated lessons for Lumen's architecture, now backed by real code (not just my earlier reasoning)

**1. Fingerprint/validate structurally, not by substring-matching a free-form field.** CodeBurn's `codex.ts` has an explicit comment: *"Validation is STRUCTURAL, never string-matching on `payload.originator`... Gating on the spelling silently dropped every third-party frontend and needed a new allowlist entry per client (issues #626, #873)."* It validates by checking the first line's `type === 'session_meta'` shape, not by scanning for a hardcoded string anywhere in the byte sample — exactly the failure mode `detect_orchestrator`'s substring-`.contains()` approach risks.

**2. Trust the orchestrator's own precomputed token totals when available — confirmed, not just my hypothesis.** `sqlite-session-parser.ts` queries `session.cost/tokens_input/tokens_output/tokens_cache_read/tokens_cache_write` directly from the DB row, exactly matching what I found querying the real `opencode.db` myself.

**3. A generic, parameterized SQLite-session-parser factory, not one bespoke parser per DB-backed tool.** `createSqliteSessionParser(source, seenKeys, config: {providerName, dbDir, dbFilePrefix})` is shared infrastructure multiple providers plug into. That's the right shape for the `SessionAdapter` trait gap I found — a second, generic ingestion path for DB-backed orchestrators, not a one-off hack for OpenCode alone.

**4. Every provider ships its own explicit tool-name mapping table.** Codex maps `exec_command`/`exec`→Bash, `read_file`→Read, `spawn_agent`/`close_agent`/`wait_agent`→Agent; Qwen maps `execute_command`→Bash, `search_files`→Grep; Kimi Code maps its own set. None of them assume one canonical tool-naming convention across ecosystems — this validates that `ToolIntent` mapping genuinely belongs *in each adapter*, per-orchestrator, not generalized away.

**5. Real production parsers handle huge lines, malformed JSON, and streaming carefully** (Codex's `session_meta` line can exceed 20KB; there's a byte-level fallback parser with bounded reads) — a level of defensive parsing rigor Lumen's adapters currently don't have.

I'm saving the meta-lesson to memory now — check real session data (or a real reference implementation like CodeBurn) *before* speccing any format-parsing logic, every time, not after. Given how much concrete, reusable knowledge is sitting in CodeBurn's `providers/` directory, want me to pull the full `codex.ts` and `opencode.ts` (plus `antigravity.ts` as a cross-check against what we already verified) and use them as the actual reference while rewriting `CodexAdapter`/`OpenCodeAdapter`, rather than working from the fragments I've grabbed so far?
